questions.question: What is the difference between var, let, and const in JavaScript? When should you use each?
questions.title: var vs let vs const in JavaScript — Scope, Hoisting & Reassignment
questions.direct_answer:
What is the difference between var, let, and const in JavaScript? When should you use each?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the type checker, emit pipeline, and how types line up with runtime JS), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Function vs block scope, hoisting differences, TDZ for let/const, reassignment vs mutation, no-redeclare rule.

**Classic weak answer:** Saying const makes the value immutable — it only makes the binding immutable; const object properties are still mutable.

**Senior finish:** Mention TDZ, no-redeclare rule of let/const, that const is the modern default (prefer-const ESLint rule), and the for-loop closure bug fix via let.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying const makes the value immutable — it only makes the binding immutable; const object properties are still mutable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention TDZ, no-redeclare rule of let/const, that const is the modern default (prefer-const ESLint rule), and the for-loop closure bug fix via let

sections.title: Why this question matters
sections.content:
This question — **var vs let vs const in JavaScript — Scope, Hoisting & Reassignment** — shows up constantly in **frontend / fullstack** interviews because it separates candidates who memorized docs from candidates who can **reason about real systems**.

**Restate the prompt:** What is the difference between var, let, and const in JavaScript? When should you use each?

A gold-level answer does four things in order:

1. **Define** the terms in plain English (what it is / what problem it solves).
2. **Explain the mechanism** (what runs when: browser, bundler, framework, network).
3. **Compare trade-offs** (speed vs correctness vs security vs DX) with **when you would not use** the default.
4. **Ground it in production** — caching, auth, observability, tests, or an incident you handled.

Interviewers are listening for: **Function vs block scope, hoisting differences, TDZ for let/const, reassignment vs mutation, no-redeclare rule**.

The fastest way to lose points is: **Saying const makes the value immutable — it only makes the binding immutable; const object properties are still mutable**.

If you only add one “senior” layer, make it: **Mention TDZ, no-redeclare rule of let/const, that const is the modern default (prefer-const ESLint rule), and the for-loop closure bug fix via let**.

sections.title: Deep dive — what to say
sections.content:
### What to explain (middle of the answer)

- **Core mechanics:** Function vs block scope, hoisting differences, TDZ for let/const, reassignment vs mutation, no-redeclare rule
- **Concrete shape:** give a small code or config snippet *only if it clarifies* (5–15 lines max).
- **Interviewer follow-ups:** expect “what breaks in production?”, “how do you debug?”, “what would you measure?” — answer them proactively.

### How to sound senior (without rambling)

- Tie the feature to **user-visible outcomes** (performance, accessibility, security).
- Mention **one failure mode** you have actually seen (race, stale cache, hydration mismatch, flaky test).
- Close with **one decision rule** (“choose X when …; choose Y when …”).

questions.question: What is hoisting in JavaScript? How does it differ for var, let, const, function declarations, and function expressions?
questions.title: JavaScript Hoisting Explained — var, let, const, Functions & TDZ
questions.direct_answer:
What is hoisting in JavaScript? How does it differ for var, let, const, function declarations, and function expressions?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the type checker, emit pipeline, and how types line up with runtime JS), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Understanding of execution-context creation phase, var initialized to undefined, full function hoisting, TDZ for let/const/class.

**Classic weak answer:** Saying let and const are not hoisted at all — they ARE hoisted but sit in the Temporal Dead Zone until declaration.

**Senior finish:** Explain the two-phase execution (creation + execution), why function declarations hoist fully but function expressions don't, and how class declarations are also in TDZ.

questions.question: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) in JavaScript?
questions.title: Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) in JavaScript — let, const & Class Hoisting
questions.direct_answer:
What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) in JavaScript?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the type checker, emit pipeline, and how types line up with runtime JS), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** let/const are hoisted but uninitialized; accessing them before declaration throws ReferenceError; TDZ also applies to class and default parameters.

**Classic weak answer:** Saying let/const are not hoisted (they are; they sit in TDZ).

**Senior finish:** Mention TDZ also applies to class declarations, default function parameters, and that typeof also throws in TDZ (unlike undeclared vars).
